15 Abstract
16 The ~289 Ma Panjal Traps of NW India (Kashmir) are part of series of rift-related mafic suites
17 (Abor, Sikkim etc.) that were erupted onto northern India (present-day coordinates) around
18 the same time as separation of the Cimmerian blocks of Qiangtang and Sibumasu. We report
19 new data from only the second paleomagnetic investigation of this unit. Standard alternating
20 field and thermal demagnetization methods were used to isolate characteristic
21 magnetizations from seven outcrops at three locations within the Kashmir Valley, NW India.
22 Analysis of four sections (14 individual cooling units) from close to Srinagar, that together
23 form a tectonically coherent sequence spanning ~3 km of stratigraphy, yield a single-
24 component, primary magnetization with a mean direction of Dec: 134.8°, Inc: 55.3° (α95 =
25 8.9°, k = 21.0). An inclination-only mean of 52.5° (α95 = 8.9°, k = 47.2) gives a paleolatitude of
26 ~33°S (± 5°). A paleopole of 110.5°E 8.4°S (A95 = 10.7) is also calculated. Assuming the
27 magnetization records a portion of the reverse polarity Kiaman Superchron, the new result
28 indicates extrusion of the Panjal Traps basalts at mid-latitudes in the southern hemisphere.
29 By inference this constrains the location of central Gondwana, and informs debates related to
30 Cimmeria’s detachment from Gondwana.
31
32
33 Keywords: Panjal Traps, Permian, paleolatitude, Greater India, Cimmerian terranes
1

### page_3
34 1. Introduction
35 The mid-Early Permian represents an important phase in Pangaea’s development marking the
36 time when the >13,000 km-long string of terranes (northern Africa-NE Arabia-northern India-
37 NW and northern Australia) collectively known as 'Cimmeria' separated from Gondwana's
38 Tethyan margin (Sengör, 1979, 1987; Sengör et al., 1988). The use of paleomagnetic data from
39 rift-related flood basalts that formed at this time provides a means to independently constrain
40 the location of India’s northern margin. As such, the data inform understanding of the
41 configuration of the eastern Cimmerian terrane along the northern Gondwana margin
42 Today, the most spectacular example of continental collision and orogenic processes is
43 the Himalayan mountain range. It is a consequence of continuing convergence between the
44 Indian and Eurasian plates that are now joined along the Indus-Yarlung-Tsangpo Suture
45 (IYTS). The timing and nature of this collision is a matter of on-going debate with estimates
46 ranging from ~65 Ma to as late as 35 Ma (Searle et al., 1987; Hodges, 2000; Aitchison et al.,
47 2007; Ali and Aitchison, 2008, 2012; Aitchison and Ali, 2012; van Hinsbergen et al., 2012a;
48 Bouilhol et al., 2013). Inextricably linked to this debate, the size of the pre-collisional India or
49 ‘Greater India’ is the center of a similar scale controversy (Ali and Aitchison, 2005, van
50 Hinsbergen et al., 2012a, 2012b; Gibbons et al., 2012). The extent of Greater India has
51 implications not only for the timing of collision with Eurasia in the Cenozoic but for our
52 understanding of how the sub-continent developed through its deeper history.
53 2. Panjal Traps and geology of the study area
54 The northern margin of India includes Late Paleozoic to Mesozoic Tethyan passive margin
55 sequences, which today form part of the Higher Himalaya (Garzanti et al., 1996a,b). During
56 the Late Carboniferous to Early Permian, terrigenous rocks were deposited in response to
57 differential uplift of the Indian margin that was linked to rifting (Vannay and Spring, 1993;
58 Garzanti et al., 1999). This extension was accompanied by eruption of the Panjal Traps, Abor
59 volcanics, Nar-Tsum spilites and Bhote Kosi basalts of the eastern and central Himalaya and
60 eventually led to the formation of the Neotethyan Ocean and the ribbon-like continent
61 Cimmeria (Acharyya, 1980; Bhat et al., 1981; Bhat, 1984; Sengör, 1987; Garzanti et al., 1999;
62 Shellnutt et al., 2011; Ali et al., 2012).
63 The Panjal Traps (Lydekker, 1883) are a suite of predominantly mafic volcanic rocks
64 that were erupted onto the Greater India portion of the Neotethyan margin (Bhat and
65 Zainuddin, 1979; Gaetani and Garzanti, 1991). They occur within the Tethyan Himalaya of NW
66 India, with the largest exposures within the Kashmir Valley and on its periphery (Bhat and
67 Zinuddin, 1979) (Figure 1). The Traps form part of the Pangaea Megasequence, conformably
2

### page_4
68 overlying pyroclastic agglomeratic shales and the freshwater, plant-bearing, siliciclastic
69 Nishatbagh beds (Wopfner and Jin, 2009). They are in turn succeeded by the Gangamopteris-
70 bearing Mamal Beds that lie directly below the Zewan Formation (Bhat and Zainuddin, 1978;
71 Kapoor and Tokuoka, 1985). Notably, the Permo-Triassic boundary occurs within the lower
72 part of the succeeding Khunamuh Formation (Kapoor and Tokuoka, 1985). The Triassic
73 sequence comprises shallow marine deposits of the Tethyan passive shelf (Bhat and
74 Zainuddin, 1978). Equivalent sections of the sequences overlying the Panjal Traps occur in the
75 Bingda-Yongde Formation redbeds of the Baoshan Block where they overlie basalts of the
76 Woniusi Formation, which are regarded as Panjal correlatives (Wang et al., 2001; Ueno, 2003).
77 Remnants of the Panjal Traps crop out from easternmost Zanskar-Spiti (East Kashmir)
78 (Fuchs, 1987; Vannay and Spring, 1993) to areas within the Western Himalayan Syntaxis in
79 NE Pakistan (Papritz and Rey, 1989) and cover a combined area >105 km2. Although their
80 original distribution remains uncertain, it has been suggested that, along with related
81 Permian volcanics in the Himalaya, their extent may have reached 0.2 x 106km2 (Ernst et al.,
82 2005). Their scale is thus similar to both the Emeishan Large Igneous Province (ELIP) of SW
83 China and the Columbia River basalts of the NW USA (Ali et al., 2005; Bryan and Ernst, 2008;
84 Shellnutt et al., 2011). The Traps consist mostly of basalts with minor basaltic-andesites,
85 rhyolites and dacites (Ganju, 1944; Nakazawa and Kapoor, 1973; Pareek, 1976; Bhat et al.,
86 1981; Shellnutt et al., 2011, 2012, 2014, 2015). Zircon LA-ICP-MS U–Pb age dating of a
87 rhyolite from the lower-middle volcanic sequence of the Panjal Traps yielded a zircon U/Pb
88 age of 289 ± 3 Ma (Shellnutt et al., 2011). The thickness of the basaltic succession ranges
89 between ~300 km in the Zanskar Range to ~3 km in the Pir Panjal Range, with individual
90 flows up to 30 m thick (Middlemiss, 1910; Wadia, 1934; Fuchs, 1987; Gaetani et al., 1990;
91 Chauvet et al., 2008). Nakazawa and Kapoor (1973) have suggested that the Panjal volcanic
92 center was located in western Kashmir because the total flow thickness is greater than other
93 regions. Most eruptions were subaerial (Wopfner and Jin, 2009) although some exposures
94 around Srinagar (i.e. Kashmir Valley) exhibit pillow structures indicating eruption in a
95 lacustrine setting (Nakazawa et al., 1975; Pareek, 1976; Bhat and Zainuddin, 1979). Silicic
96 volcanic rocks are concentrated within the Kashmir valley beneath the basalt flows and
97 appear to be restricted to the Pir Panjal Range (Ganju, 1944; Shellnutt et al., 2012). The
98 stratigraphic position of the silicic units is somewhat unusual in that they occur as the lower
99 flows whereas in other LIPs they are typically found in the waning sequences (Sheth, 2007).
3

### page_5
100 In terms of the geotectonic setting in which the traps were erupted, Detailed
101 geochemical studies have identified signatures typical of tholeiitic OIB/P-MORB-type basalts
102 consistent with a rifting scenario (Vannay and Spring, 1993; Chauvet et al., 2008).
103 However, the specific mechanism that initiated the rifting has not been fully resolved.
104 Geological and large-scale paleogeographical relationships suggest a passive rifting scenario
105 resulting from increasing slab-pull forces in the Paleotethys following the subduction of a
106 mid-oceanic ridge beneath the Eurasian margin to the north (Gaetani and Garzanti, 1991;
107 Stampfli et al., 1991, Garzanti et al., 1996; Stampfli and Borel, 2002). An alternative scenario
108 invokes the involvement of a Tethyan mantle plume forming the Arabia-India-Cimmeria triple
109 junction (Lapierre et al., 2004Chauvet et al., 2009;).
110 The spatio-temporal association between the extrusion of the Panjal Traps and the
111 rifting of the Cimmerian terranes is important for determining the location of the rifting
112 margin. Chauvet et al., (2008) suggested that the Traps erupted during the Middle to Late
113 Permian. More recent U/Pb zircon dating work by Shellnutt et al. (2011) has yielded an Early
114 Permian age of ~289 Ma. Thus, the Traps form the locus of the India-Cimmeria rifting margin
115 and potentially may provide a paleolatitudinal constraint for defining the extent of Greater
116 India.
117 3. Paleomagnetic investigation
118 3.1 Previous work
119 McElhinny et al. (1978) reported paleomagnetic data from thirteen flows collected in the
120 vicinity of Srinagar during a 1967 Geological Survey of India expedition From twelve of these
121 samples that were subjected to a detailed step-wise demagnetization (alternating field and
122 thermal) they reported a mean magnetization of Dec: 156.5° Inc: 32.5° (α95 = 9.9°, k = 19.8, n
123 = 12), and a resulting paleopole of 32°N 282°E. The samples yielded a positive fold test,
124 suggesting magnetization during Early Tertiary Himalayan uplift McElhinny et al. (1978)
125 They noted similarity between Panjal and the Tertiary Deccan Traps poles (Wensink, 1973)
126 but apparent disparity with other Permian poles from the Salt Range, Pakistan (Wensink,
127 1975) and the Indian Peninsular shield (Wensink, 1968; Klootwijk, 1975). McElhinny et al.
128 (1978) concluded that their mean magnetization was likely an overprint acquired during the
129 formation of the Himalayas’. Detailed review of the McElhinny et al. (1978) suggest potential
130 problems that could affect the tectonic interpretation, in particular some directions may not
131 have been appropriately corrected for bedding. Six of the 12 sample sites presented by
132 McElhinny et al. (1978) had no bedding correction applied which, considering the proximity
4

### page_6
133 of these sites to the significantly tilted beds of our sampled horizons (dip = 33-43°), casts
134 doubt on their reliability.
135 3.2 Present study
136 3.2.1 Introduction
137 The primary objective of our investigation was to gain robust magnetic remanence to
138 constrain the location of the Neotethyan rifting margin between NW Greater India and the
139 adjacent portion of the Cimmerian terrane.
140 3.2.2 Sampling locations
141 The main sampling was conducted in Srinagar and the nearby Kashmir Valley, NW India. In
142 addition, material was collected from Sonamarg, ~40 km NE of Srinagar, and the Aharbal Falls
143 area ~60 km south of Srinagar, but they did not yield useful/consistent data, thus these
144 locations will not be discussed further.
145 3.2.2.1 Locality One: Guryul Ravine and SE Srinagar quarries (Outcrops PT1-PT4)
146 The type locality for the Panjal Traps includes exposures in the Kashmir Valley, specifically
147 those close to Srinagar (Wopfner and Jin, 2009; Huddleston, 1896, Lydekker, 1883). Several
148 quarries near the town of Pampore ~9 km southeast of Srinagar augment the natural
149 exposures. Together, the exposures and workings allow access a quasi-continuous several
150 km-thick, 30-40° dipping stratigraphic succession of Panjal Trap flows and associated strata,
151 from silicic units at the base to the overlying Middle-Upper Permian and Triassic sediments.
152 Samples were collected from the Guryul Ravine (PT1) and three adjacent quarries (PT2, PT3
153 and PT4). The total thickness of the basalt-dominated section is ~3300 m. The unit is
154 underlain by ~1300 m of silicic volcanic rocks. Individual flows up to 30 m thick (Chauvet et
155 al., 2008; Shellnutt et al., 2011) dominate the succession. Columnar jointing and the presence
156 of plant fossils in rare interbeds indicate subaerial eruption. Pillow lavas at Guryul Ravine are
157 interpreted to indicate eruption in a lacustrine setting (Nakazawa and Kapoor 1973). The
158 uppermost flows are brecciated and conformably overlain by the Gangamopteris beds, which
159 comprise tuffaceous chert and shale. The basaltic rocks are fresh although some have
160 experienced zeolite facies metamorphism.
161 Together exposures from outcrops PT1-PT4 form a tectonically continuous and
162 coherent sequence of beds. Thus, we treat the paleomagnetic results from this region as those
163 of a single locality for purposes of determining a formation-mean direction. From analogy to
164 studies of eruption patterns associated with similar LIPs (Renne and Basu, 1991; Richards et
165 al., 1989), we estimate that the ~3 km thick composite section would have been erupted over
5

### page_7
166 1-2 m.y. As such this should be sufficient to allow for geomagnetic secular variation to be
167 averaged.
168 3.2.2.1.1 Outcrop PT1: Guryul Ravine
169 The Guryul Ravine (074°56.69' E 34°04.54' N) is a classic exposure particularly known for
170 Permo-Triassic sediments. It is especially significant for sediments that preserve the
171 biostratigraphical and paleoclimatological signatures characterizing the Permo-Triassic
172 extinction (Sweet, 1970; Matsuda, 1981; Korte et al., 2010). These rocks conformably rest
173 upon the uppermost flows of the Panjal Traps. Critically, the succession demonstrates the
174 nature of the transition from rift to post-rift passive margin regimes that evolved during
175 rifting of eastern Cimmeria from the Indian margin of Gondwana (Gaetani and Garzanti, 1991;
176 Metcalfe, 1994). These upper basaltic flows have been a focus of several studies including
177 (Shellnutt et al., 2011, 2012, 2014, 2015). It is interesting to note that it was not included, or
178 at least not explicitly identified, as a sampling locality in the study by McElhinny et al. (1978).
179 However, it is a possible that the Guryul lavas are correlative of flows at some of their sites e.g.
180 the Atwai Quarries. Strata at Outcrop PT1 dip ~43° towards the ESE (115°). The flows here
181 are 2-3 m thick dark, largely aphanitic, cooling units with tabular boundaries. Primarily
182 basaltic, they were likely to have been erupted sub-aerially (Wopfner and Jin, 2009). There is
183 evidence of epidote alteration, probably penecontemporaneous with eruption and cooling.
184 Some cooling units contain small but abundant veins of quartz and epidote ~5 cm thick;
185 others exhibit ‘jigsaw’ brecciation. Such flows were avoided as they present difficulties with
186 sample extraction. Four block samples (PT1.1-1.4) were collected from discrete cooling units,
187 and span ~15 m of the stratigraphy.
188 3.2.2.1.2 Outcrop PT2: Zewan quarry
189 This outcrop is a small abandoned quarry SW of Guryul Ravine near Zewan (074°54.72' E
190 34°03.07' N). The bedding attitude is similar to that of Guryul Ravine, that is ~40° to the SE,
191 but the exposure is less extensive. The sequence is estimated to lie ~1 km lower in the
192 stratigraphic succession than that of the Guryul Ravine. Cooling units are typically 2-3 m thick
193 massive basalt flows with tabular boundaries. The lowermost flows are amygdaloidal with
194 epidote infilling. Four block samples (PT2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4) were collected from this site and
195 span ~20 m of stratigraphy.
196 3.2.2.1.3 Outcrop PT3: Athwajan Quarry
197 This locality is a large working quarry adjacent to the village of Athwajan, ~5 km west of
198 Zewan (074°52.28' E 34°02.77' N). Cooling units are 3-4 m thick flows with tabular
199 boundaries. The overall orientation of the units is ~43° towards the south. Notably the rocks
6

### page_8
200 are slightly more felsic than those at in the previous two. Stratigraphically these flows are
201 from the lower part of the Panjal Traps (Shellnutt et al., 2012) approximately 3 km lower in
202 the section than those at Guryul Ravine. Samples were preferentially collected from massive,
203 aphanitic sections of individual cooling units. Although oriented blocks were collected from
204 five flows (PT 3.1-3.5) spanning 30-40 m of stratigraphic succession, PT3.4 did not survive the
205 journey to the laboratory and thus could not be analyzed.
206 3.2.3.1.4 Outcrop PT4: Pantha Chowk Quarry
207 The locality is a large working quarry near Pantha Chowk (074°53.01' E 34°02.40' N) and is
208 close to Outcrop PT3. It was the primary sample site of the Shellnutt et al. (2011) that
209 successfully extracted zircons for radiometric dating (289 ±3 Ma). Samples from the ‘Atwai
210 Quarries near Srinagar town’ described by McElhinny et al. (1978) are most likely from either
211 or both the Athwajan and Pantha Chowk quarries although this cannot be affirmed with
212 certainty. Bedding attitude is 37° to the SE and the characteristically 1-3 m thick cooling units
213 have tabular boundaries similar to those elsewhere. Four block samples were collected at this
214 site (PT 4.1 - PT 4.4) across a 30-40 m of stratigraphy.
215 3.2.3 Sampling method
216 At each outcrop oriented blocks (ideally within ±2° in both the horizontal and vertical planes),
217 500–700 cm3, were collected from discrete cooling units (all bar one are flows, the other is a
218 gabbroic dyke). Each individual cooling-unit block sample, therefore, represents a
219 paleomagnetic ‘site’ because the sample should provide an instantaneous record of the
220 geomagnetic field a shortly after the magma had crystallized and the magnetic grains cooled
221 below their blocking temperatures. There is, however, potential for blocks collected in this
222 way to record small sampling-related orientation biases, which is not really a problem with
223 field-based drill-cored collections. Therefore, in an attempt to minimize this effect, we aimed
224 to select reference surfaces with very different orientations to the others in the section.
225 Magnetic bearings were corrected to ‘true’ using the International Geomagnetic Field Model,
226 version 11; at the time of sampling the offset was ∼1°W.
227 3.2.4 Laboratory methodology
228 The bulk of the samples were prepared and analyzed at the University of Hong Kong
229 Paleomagnetic Laboratory. Blocks were set in plaster-of-Paris and six to eight 2.54-cm-
230 diameter by 2.15 cm-long core specimens were drilled from each block. A total of 29 block
231 samples were collected yielding ~165 mini-cores of which 126 were analysed.
232 The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each prepared specimens was measured using
233 an AGICO JR-6A spinner magnetometer. In order to determine the magnetization history of
7

### page_9
234 the samples, a stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization was carried at steps varying
235 between 2.5 and 10 mT using a “Molspin Tumbler” (which has a peak field of 100 mT).
236 Examples of demagnetization behavior are presented in Figure 2.
237 For those specimens that did not respond to the AF treatment (e.g., Figure 2, Specimen
238 PT4-4B), they were then subjected to thermal demagnetization. This work was carried out
239 using an ASC Scientific (TD 48SC) thermal specimen demagnetizer at the Australian National
240 University RSES Black Mountain Paleomagnetic laboratory. The demagnetization steps were
241 50°C between 250 and 400°C; 33°C steps from 400 to 500°C; . 20-25°C beyond 500°C until
242 total NRM was removed. Examples showing the demagnetization behavior are shown in
243 Figure 3. Most sample yielded simple magnetization histories, but some displaying ‘noisy’,
244 erratic results and these were excluded from any analysis. Data were subsequently analysed
245 with software developed by Core Magnetics Ltd. UK and CEMP Systems Pmag Tools 4.2a
246 (Hounslow, 2006).
247 Characteristic magnetization directions were determined using principal component
248 analysis (Kirschvink 1980) applied to data plotted on vector-endpoint plots (Zijderveld 1967).
249 Typically, a stable single direction is observed above 10–20 mT/350–400°C. Thermal
250 demagnetization indicates these directions are recorded either by magnetite (because they
251 ‘unblock’ ≤578°C, followed by a sharp decline in intensity) or magnetite plus variable
252 fractions of haematite (which unblocks ≤680°C). Block-sample- and locality-mean directions
253 were calculated using Fisher (1953) statistics.
254 We consider the magnetite record to represent a primary signal, whereas any haematite
255 component is an alteration remanance acquired shortly afterwards, very possibly before the
256 next flow.
257 3.2.5 Results
258 3.2.5.1 Outcrop PT1: Guryul Ravine
259 Five mini-cores from each block, with the exception mini-core 4 from PT1.2, were first treated
260 using AF demagnetization. Two additional specimens from each block were subsequently
261 subjected to thermal demagnetization. NRM intensities ranged from 240 to 2100 mA/m. in
262 samples PT1.1, 1.2, 1.3, a viscous remanence was removed at ≤ 8 mT. Beyond this, samples
263 carried a single-component magnetization with median destructive fields between 6-10 mT
264 with a reversed polarity. All PT1 samples reached unblocking temperatures between 550°C
265 and 600°C suggesting that the remanence is carried by magnetite. While characteristic
266 magnetization directions were identified for the PT1.4 specimens, the scatter in directions
8

### page_10
267 was deemed too large (α95 = 22.0°, k = 10.0) thus the mean direction was not used in
268 calculating the exposure mean.
269 3.2.5.2 Outcrop PT2: Zewan Quarry
270 Five mini-core specimens from blocks PT 2.1 and 2.3 and four from blocks PT 2.2 and 2.4
271 were treated initially using AF demagnetization. As a consequence of two specimens each
272 from PT 2.1 and 2.3 and one specimen from PT 2.2 and 2.4 not responding to the treatment,
273 they were later subjected to thermal demagnetization where unblocking was achieved at 550-
274 600°C . NRM intensities ranged from relatively low in PT2.1 (7.3 to 9 mA/m) to very high 160-
275 940 mA/m in PT2.2 with intermediate values in PT2.3 (13-33 mA/m) and PT2.4 (13-52
276 mA/m). The large range in NRM suggests varying concentrations of magnetic minerals but
277 consistent directions were recorded nonetheless with median destructive fields between 6-8
278 mT. Although plots for mini-core specimens from PT2.1 are ‘noisy’ due to low magnetic
279 intensities, consistent single-component remanences with reversed polarity were isolated in
280 all block samples.
281 3.2.5.3 Outcrop PT3: Athwajan Quarry
282 Five specimens from each block sample, excluding PT3.5, were AF demagnetized. Two
283 additional specimens (only one from PT3.1) from each block were subsequently subjected to
284 thermal demagnetization where unblocking occurred at 550-600°C. In PT3.1, 3.2, 3.3, NRM
285 intensities ranged from 1.3 - 120 mA/m. Pilot specimens from PT 3.5 returned intensities so
286 low (0.01-0.73 mA/m) as to be out of the reliable range of the magnetometer. Consequently,
287 ChRMs could be isolated and specimens from this block were not tested beyond the pilot
288 measurements. From the remaining samples, specimen analysis plots indicating a prominent
289 single magnetization component with a reversed polarity. A single mini-core specimen from
290 PT3.3 (PT3.3b) returned an anomalous direction (possibly due to a sampling error) and was
291 excluded from the sample mean calculation.
292 3.2.5.4 Outcrop Pt4: Pantha Chowk Quarry
293 Five specimens drilled from blocks PT4.1 and 4.2 were satisfactorily demagnetized using AF
294 with two additional mini-core specimens subjected to thermal demagnetization, again with
295 unblocking at 550-600°C. The pilot samples from PT 4.3 and 4.4 did not respond to the
296 treatment and thus all of the cores from these blocks were subjected to thermal
297 demagnetization. Unsurprisingly, these all unblocked at 680°C and 700°C (indicative of a
298 hematite carrier). NRM intensities ranged from 0.7-17.7 mA/m. Despite ‘noisy’ plots due to
299 low intensities, specimens from PT4.1 and 4.2 yielded single component, reverse-polarity
9

### page_11
300 remanences. The specimens from PT 4.3 and 4.4 also bore single directions similar to those of
301 PT4.1 and 4.2.
302 3.2.6 Calculating a formation mean direction
303 Treating the four localities as (PT1-4) as a tectonically coherent section, a Fisher mean
304 direction calculation for all samples, excluding PT 1.4 and 3.5, gives a locality mean of Dec:
305 134.8°, Inc: 55.3°, where α95 = 8.9° and k = 21.0 with n =14; Figure 4). An inclination only
306 mean, using the statistics of McFadden and Reid (1982), gives Inc =52.5°, where α95 = 4.9°
307 and k = 47.2 with n = 14).
308 3.2.7. Discussion
309 The single-component nature of these fourteen PT1-4 outcrop flows leaves two avenues open
310 for interpretation: (1) the magnetization is primary and that this particular exposure of the
311 Panjal Traps, in contrast to the other outcrops in Kashmir has been spared from alteration
312 and overprinting; (2) the original magnetization has been completely overprinted throughout
313 the entire block during a later event as suggested by McElhinny et al. (1978).
314 Consistency of results is demonstrated with general agreement in results over both a
315 significant stratigraphic and areal range. Although the amount of spread between results
316 through the stratigraphy is appreciable it is not unacceptable. Indeed the directional scatter
317 suggests that magnetizations were acquired and different times by successive flows and
318 record fluctuations in the geomagnetic field over the eruption period spanning a few million
319 years, and are thus primary. Critically, a tighter grouping would suggest a much younger,
320 ‘wholesale’ overprint acquired simultaneously at all depths over a relatively short period. A
321 primary magnetization scenario thus seems to be the most parsimonious interpretation. The
322 tilt-corrected mean is (Dec: 134.8°, Inc: 55.3°, α95 = 8.9°, k = 21.0, n =14) yields a paleopole
323 (south) of 110.5°E 8.4°S (A95 = 10.7). As paleolatitude is derived from inclination alone, the
324 inclination-only mean is 52.5° (α95 = 4.9, k = 47.2, n = 14) (McFadden and Reid, 1982).
325 Assuming that the signal is primary and given the Early Permian Gondwana context of the
326 Panjal Traps, this yields a paleolatitude of 33.1 ±5° S.
327 Considering northern India’s position in the mid-latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere during
328 the Permian, the magnetization is interpreted to be of reversed polarity. Therefore the tilt-
329 corrected mean direction cannot be a recent acquisition as it is not consistent with the
330 present field (Tauxe, 2010). Consistency between varying NRM intensities and mineralogies,
331 magnetite and hematite, suggests that the hematite formed shortly after crystallization.
332 Usually, a primary magnetization plot will show significantly tighter grouping after bedding
333 correction. However, in this case the reduction in scatter is small.
10

### page_12
334 3.2.7.1 Comparison to previous studies
335 Given the significant contrast of these new data with the earlier study of McElhinny et al.
336 (1978) comparison between the two is warranted. It may be noted that the new and old
337 datasets both plot with the same polarity and in the same quadrant. Indeed, the mean
338 declination varies by only 16°. The main discrepancy is in the inclination means with those
339 reported by McElhinny et al. (1987) being significantly shallower at 32.2° (α95 = 9.0°, k = 17).
340 This inclination corresponds to a paleolatitude of ~17.5°, thus the suggestion that
341 magnetization was a ‘Tertiary overprint’.
342 Interestingly, McElhinny et al. (1978) report a positive fold test but the location of the folded
343 strata used is not given. As such structures were not observed at the sample sites visited in
344 this study, it is surmised that at least some of the sample sites used in their study have a
345 distinctly different structure to the Guryul volcanic pile. While inconsistencies in the earlier
346 dataset have been approached forensically, inevitably some degree of speculation may be
347 introduced. One suspected “problem” is that the bedding corrections were not fully applied in
348 the earlier work. Whatever the explanation, this is ultimately impossible to determine without
349 the essential basic geological data of their sampling sites, which the 1978 publication lacks.
350 3.3 Implications
351 The orientation of magnetization in the Panjal Traps is consistent with the
352 Sakmarian/Artinskian age of the unit which is well constrained both stratigraphically
353 (Wopfner and Jin, 2009) and radiometrically (289 ±3 Ma) (Shellnutt et al., 2011). Importantly,
354 the reversed polarity of the magnetization is consistent with the accepted geomagnetic
355 orientation for this age corresponding to the ∼318-262Ma Kiaman Reverse Polarity
356 Superchron (Opdyke et al., 2000, Cottrell et al., 2008, Irving and Parry, 1963).
357 The inclination-only mean of magnetization, 52.5° (α95 = 4.9°), indicates eruption occurred at
358 mid-latitudes ~33.1°S (error range is 42.5°S to 25.5°S) (Figure 5). The Panjal Traps thus
359 erupted during rifting of the Qiantiang and western Lhasa terranes at this latitude. This
360 constrains the position of the relevant portion of the Early Permian Neotethyan margin, and
361 by inference fixes the maximum extent of NW Greater India. These data are consistent with
362 eastern Cimmerian configurations inferred from the paleomagnetic data of the Baoshan
363 terrane (Ali et al., 2013). The direct association between extrusion of the Panjal Traps and the
364 exact configuration of the Qiangtang, Sibumasu and Lhasa terranes in this region is yet to be
365 established. Basalts in the Karakoram postulated to be related to this rifting may provide such
366 a point of correlation (Rao and Rai, 2007), however, their equivalence to the Panjal Traps is
367 yet to be determined. Using a global reference frame model (Torsvik et al. 2008)
11

### page_13
368 reconstruction back to the early Permian (~280 Ma) there is ~8° of separation between
369 cratonic India and the inferred site the Panjal Traps rifting center constrained to 33°S.
370 With regard to the extent of Greater India, the review paper of Ali & Aitchison (2005)
371 suggested that the extension to the NW of the craton was ~900 km. This is somewhat larger
372 than estimates for the Western Syntaxis area of ~600 km given by models using the Wallaby-
373 Zenith constraint but is consistent with the estimate of ~950 km for the central areas (Ali and
374 Aitchison, 2005, 2006; Gibbons et al., 2012). Assuming that main eruptive center for the
375 Panjal Traps is within the Kashmir Valley, somewhat east of the Western Syntaxis, and further
376 south relative the IYTS, this discrepancy may be accommodated. Notably, the possible ~10°
377 range indicated by the error probability ellipse (± 4.9°) introduces an uncertainty up to 1,100
378 km. Necessarily this places significant limitations on the conclusions we may draw solely from
379 these data. Thus our inferences remain indicative rather than conclusive.
380 3.4 Comparison to other Late Paleozoic poles for India
381 Direct comparison with other Permian Indian poles is difficult, if not impossible, due to a lack
382 of reliable data for this region and period. Several studies report Late Paleozoic poles from
383 Himalayan and Peninsula India, the majority dating to the 1970s and 1980s (e.g. Klootwijk,
384 1975, Klootwijk et al., 1983). However, as none are included within the IAGA Global
385 Paleomagnetic Database (Pisarevsky, 2005) this suggests limited reliability for these results.
386 The only pole currently listed in the IAGA database and in use in modern reconstructive
387 tectonic references frames (Torsvik et al., 2008, 2012; Van der Voo, 1993) is that derived from
388 the Alozai Formation of Baluchistan, NE Pakistan (111°E 18.1°N) (Klootwijk et al., 1981).
389 Besides being of questionable reliability (α95 = 12.1° but with k = 6.0), deeper investigation of
390 the provenance of the paleomagnetic data shows that the assumed ~280 Ma age (271-318 Ma
391 in the IAGA Database, 289.5 Ma in Torsvik et al., (2008)) of the unit was poorly constrained at
392 the time of that particular paleomagnetic investigation, having been placed within a very
393 broad range of ‘Permo-Carboniferous to Liassic’ (Klootwijk et al., 1981). More recently, the
394 Alozai Group has been reassigned with some confidence to a Middle and Lower Jurassic age
395 (Maldonado et al., 2011). This pole is thus rejected as representative of the Early Permian.
396 Consequently, a pole derived from the new Panjal Traps data might thus be said to represent
397 the only robust paleomagnetic dataset from northern India of Late Paleozoic age.
398 4. Conclusions
399 Tectonic reconstructions of Gondwana back to the Early Permian are constrained using global
400 hybrid data with the assumption that relationships between South Africa, Madagascar, and
401 India are fixed during this time (Torsvik et al., 2012). The relevance of our new Early Permian
12

### page_14
402 paleomagnetic data for India lies in their potential to constrain the breakaway Cimmerian
403 components of the Neotethyan margin. Our study highlights the potential for key geological
404 constraints such as age and structural data to be overlooked when dealing with the large,
405 global dataset allowing the incorporation of erroneous results. Conversely, there is also
406 potential for immediately relevant data or resources to be dismissed. The new, primary
407 paleomagnetic data from the Panjal Traps reported here represents a contribution to the
408 larger Indian and, indeed, global paleomagnetic dataset filling a gap in the record for Early
409 Permian India and Gondwana.
410 The results of this study and its conclusions are bound by significant limitations due to
411 the small sample size arising from local insurgency that made circumstances difficult for
412 fieldwork at the time. Nevertheless, the data are indicative of the potential of the Panjal Traps,
413 and other Cimmerian rift basalt sequences, to yield paleomagnetic data that have significant
414 implications for the nature of the Greater Indian Neotethyan margin and its evolution through
415 time.

659 (Torsvik et al. (2008) after Ali et al. (2012). Extrusion location of the Panjal Traps is plotted
660 according to the paleolatitude constraint calculated in this study (33°S ± 4.9°) and in
661 accordance with the inferred configuration of the eastern Cimmerian terranes. The sample
662 site (locality 1) is plotted at corresponding present-day coordinates on cratonic India. The
663 disparity between the two was calculated to be ~8°.

### page_23
*Highlights (for review)
• The Early Permian Panjal Traps erupted at a latitude of ~33°S (± 5°)
• Location of India and its western Neotethyan margin constrained
• Paleomagnetic data from Kashmir eastwards through to Baoshan increase
understanding of Gondwana breakup and dispersal of Cimmerian terranes
